title: RUNNING MAN - Learn In 2 Minutes | Dance Moves In Minutes

method.teacher_system: The teacher breaks down the movement into small, manageable chunks, starting with a simple jump-split. He then adds the specific footwork and timing, and finally introduces a stylistic variation to complete the move.
method.signature: The teacher uses a very specific, simple, and repetitive breakdown of the footwork that makes the move accessible to non-dancers.

practices.what: The teacher demonstrates the jump-split movement, breaking it down into two distinct parts: jumping into a split and then jumping feet together.
The teacher leads the learner through several repetitions of the basic jump-split movement, counting out loud to help with the rhythm.
The teacher adds the detail of lifting the back foot during the jump-split movement to refine the technique.
The teacher introduces a stylistic variation by sliding the front leg back, adding a more fluid and dance-like quality to the movement.

adaptations.difficulty: The basic hopping movement may feel too simple or lack style.
adaptations.adjustment: The teacher suggests sliding the front leg back to add style.

moments.says: The teacher introduces the running man as an essential dance move that has spanned generations.
The teacher breaks down the move by facing the side and explaining the footwork step by step.
The teacher invites the learner to repeat the basic footwork a couple of times.
The teacher explains that the back foot must be lifted up when jumping the feet together.
The teacher encourages the learner to break the move down slowly and go back if needed.
The teacher offers a variation to add style by sliding the front leg back.
The teacher encourages the learner to master the move and use it at parties or events.

mentor.what_stays: The teacher leaves the learner feeling capable of mastering a classic dance move through practice.

struggles.theme: Difficulty with foot sliding and coordination

clicked.theme: Clear breakdown of the first step

method.limits: The video only shows a side view, which may limit the learner's ability to see the movement from other angles.
